opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the ideas I'm most excited about, because the core problem with evaluating scalable oversight is that you're trying to measure whether humans, with AI assistance, can supervise tasks they couldn't evaluate on their own. And if they can't evaluate the tasks themselves, how do you know whether the assistance is actually helping, or whether it's just making them more confident while they're still wrong?

Code gives you a nice way around that. You take a piece of code that works correctly, and you deliberately introduce a bug, ideally a subtle one that's hard to spot. Now you have ground truth: you know there's a flaw and you know exactly where it is. Then you give it to someone and ask them to find the problem, or just to judge whether the code is fine.

You can run it almost like a randomized controlled trial. One group of evaluators looks at the code unassisted. Another group gets help from an AI system, say a model trained to write critiques pointing out problems. Then you measure how often each group finds the bug. If the assisted group catches significantly more of the planted bugs, that's evidence your oversight technique is actually extending what humans can reliably evaluate.

What makes this useful is that you can also make it adversarial. You can have a model try to insert bugs that are as hard as possible to detect, and another model try to help humans find them. That gives you a sense of how the technique holds up against something actively trying to fool the overseer, which is closer to the situation we eventually worry about.

You also get to look at the failure modes. Does the assistant point out lots of nitpicks and the human gets overwhelmed? Does it hallucinate problems that aren't there? Since you know where the real bug is, you can measure both catching real flaws and not raising false alarms.

There are limitations. Planted bugs might not be representative of the bugs that naturally occur, and of course we eventually care about tasks much harder than code review. But as a testbed where you have ground truth and can iterate quickly, it's really valuable, because otherwise you're often stuck just hoping the oversight works without a way to check.

r003.rationale: It proposes testing oversight against difficult-to-detect bugs, but does not measure how easy it is to introduce bugs that evade oversight.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so the basic problem with scalable oversight is that you want to know whether your oversight technique actually works on tasks that are too hard for humans to evaluate directly. And the obvious difficulty is: if humans can't evaluate the task, how do you know whether the oversight got the right answer? You've got nothing to check against.

So one approach I'm quite excited about is what we sometimes call "sandwiching" or targeted perturbations, and code is a really nice domain for this. The idea is pretty simple. You take some codebase, and you deliberately introduce bugs into it. Subtle ones, ideally. You know exactly where the bugs are because you put them there. Then you ask the model to do a code review, or you have the model write code and you've asked it to insert a bug that's hard to find, and then you see whether your oversight process — whether that's a human assisted by another model, or a debate setup, or a critique model — actually catches it.

The nice thing is you now have ground truth. You know the bug is there. So you can measure a detection rate. And you can vary the difficulty: make the bugs subtler, put them in bigger codebases, put them in domains where the human reviewer has less expertise, and see where the oversight process starts to break down.

Even better, you can set it up adversarially. You can have one model that's trying to insert bugs that won't be noticed, and you have your oversight process trying to catch them. And that's actually a pretty close analogue to the situation we're really worried about, which is: what if the model is subtly sandbagging or inserting vulnerabilities on purpose, and we don't notice? If your oversight can't catch bugs that a model deliberately planted in a setting where you know they exist, you should be pretty worried about relying on it when you don't know.

The other thing I like about code is that it's somewhere the models are already really capable, and it's a domain we care about enormously from a safety perspective, because models are going to be writing a lot of the code that runs the world, and a lot of the code that trains the next models. So it's not an artificial toy task. The thing you're measuring is actually close to the thing you'd deploy.

There are caveats, of course. The bugs you insert might not be representative of the bugs a scheming model would insert. And models might be able to tell when they're in a test setting. But as a first-order measurement of "does my oversight signal actually track correctness when the task gets hard," I think it's one of the more concrete and tractable things you can do right now.

r002.rationale: It proposes having a model deliberately insert bugs into code and testing whether an oversight process catches them.

r003.rationale: It describes an adversarial model inserting bugs intended to go unnoticed and varying their subtlety to measure where oversight breaks down.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss a discriminator flagging code without a critique model identifying the bug, or what that would reveal.

astra-6.text:
One thing you could do is take a piece of code and deliberately insert a bug, and then ask your oversight process to find it. You know the bug is there because you put it there, but the person doing the evaluation doesn’t know where it is. Then you can compare how well a human does on their own with how well they do with AI assistance.

The interesting cases are ones where the bug is hard for the human to find or understand unaided. Can the AI point them to the relevant part of the code, explain what goes wrong, and help them construct a test that demonstrates the problem? That gives you something concrete to check, beyond whether the explanation sounds convincing.

You could also have one model introduce bugs and another model help the human find them. That lets you make the task adversarial: the first model is trying to produce a change that looks reasonable but has a subtle flaw.

Of course, success on deliberately inserted bugs wouldn’t establish that scalable oversight works in general. The bugs might be unrepresentative, or the models might share blind spots. But it gives you a controlled setting where you can start measuring whether assistance actually enables people to oversee things they couldn’t reliably oversee otherwise.

r003.rationale: The adversarial example involves a subtle flaw, but the response does not propose measuring how easy it is to introduce bugs that evade oversight.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe a discriminator flagging buggy code without a critique model identifying the bug.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing you could do is take a piece of code and deliberately insert a bug that’s quite hard to find. Then you ask a human, assisted by an AI system, to review the code. Can they find the bug? Can they explain what goes wrong and under what circumstances?

The nice thing about this setup is that you know where the bug is, so you have a way to check whether the oversight succeeded. But you don’t have to give that information to the person doing the review. You can then compare how well they do with different kinds of AI assistance, or with no assistance at all.

And you’d want to make the task increasingly difficult: larger codebases, subtler bugs, things that require understanding how different parts interact. The important question is whether the assistance lets the human reliably catch problems they couldn’t have caught on their own. Finding deliberately inserted bugs wouldn’t by itself establish that scalable oversight works in general, but it gives you a concrete setting where you can measure progress.

r002.rationale: It proposes inserting a bug and testing human review with AI assistance, but does not say a trained model introduces the bug.

r003.rationale: It recommends increasing task difficulty, but does not propose measuring how easily bugs can be introduced that evade oversight.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss a discriminator flagging buggy code or a critique model failing to identify the bug.
